system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2175-10-20 21:05:00 to 2175-10-21 10:30:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: James, a 60-year-old man with a history of alcohol use disorder, COPD, chronic pain from prior trauma, and hypertension, was admitted after being found unresponsive and intoxicated. He presented with hypotension and hypoxia, which improved with IV fluids and oxygen support. His condition was complicated by a high blood alcohol level, somnolence, and prior noncompliance with treatment. A chest X-ray showed chronic emphysematous changes and bibasilar atelectasis without acute pneumonia. He received one dose of levofloxacin in the emergency department but did not complete a full course. Due to agitation, he required Haldol and brief physical restraints. Despite plans to initiate detox and pursue a Section 35 hold, James insisted on leaving against medical advice. He was alert and ambulatory at discharge, with understanding of the risks, and was advised to seek follow-up care.
problems: Acute alcoholic intoxication in alcoholism, unspecified
Chronic airway obstruction, not elsewhere classified

___.

FINDINGS:  Single AP upright portable view of the chest was obtained.  There
is mild elevation of the hemidiaphragm.  Overlying right base linear opacity
most likely represents subsegmental atelectasis.  Subtle patchy left lower
lung opacity is seen, difficult to discern whether lingular or left lower lobe
on this single frontal view.  No large pleural effusion or pneumothorax.  The
cardiac and mediastinal silhouettes are stable.  External artifact is seen
projecting over the medial lung fields.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Patchy left lower lung opacity, not definitely seen on the prior study
concerning for infection and/or aspiration.  Elevation of the right
hemidiaphragm and right base atelectasis.

CHEST RADIOGRAPH

INDICATION:  Pulmonary exam, pulmonary edema, COPD.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:  As compared to the previous radiograph, there is no relevant
change.  Minimal improvement of the known right basal atelectasis.  Unchanged
size of the cardiac silhouette.  Unchanged minimal retrocardiac atelectasis. 
No overt pulmonary edema.  Unchanged minimal flattening of the left
hemidiaphragm.

diagnoses.long_title: Acute alcoholic intoxication in alcoholism, continuous

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Patel. You're here because you were found sleeping at the T station and brought in with low oxygen. Can I ask your name?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: James. Yeah, I know. I had a few drinks. I’m fine now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, James. Your oxygen was in the 80s when you arrived, which is low. We’ve put you on high-flow oxygen to help you breathe better. You also have COPD, so we need to be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know my lungs aren’t great. But I don’t feel short of breath now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, but your chest X-ray shows some changes — a possible infection or worsening of your COPD. We’re treating you for both with antibiotics and steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want any more meds. I’ve been in and out of here too much already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but you’re at risk because of your alcohol use and lung condition. We’re concerned you might not be able to care for yourself safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can take care of myself. I just need to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: James, your labs show your white blood cell count is low, and your blood is slightly acidic. We’re watching you closely in the ICU tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. More tests. I feel like a guinea pig.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re trying to help. Your blood work also shows you’re retaining CO2, which is common in COPD. That’s why we’re giving you oxygen carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. The repeat chest X-ray shows no major changes. Your oxygen levels are now normal on room air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We were going to start formal alcohol detox and possibly file for a Section 35 hold because of your repeated hospitalizations and safety concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not staying. I know the risks. I’m leaving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You do have the right to leave, but I need to make sure you understand it’s dangerous, especially with your history of alcohol dependence and lung disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I’m still leaving. I’ll follow up if I need to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’ll discharge you against medical advice. Please go to the emergency department if you feel worse — short of breath, confused, or very unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send the discharge papers. Please consider reaching out to addiction services. Your health depends on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll think about it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: James, just confirming — you’re leaving now, and you understand the risks of not completing treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I understand. I’m leaving on my own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You’re discharged. Take care, James.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will assist you with discharge paperwork. Please call if you need help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, James. Stay safe.

summary.summary_paragraph: James, a 60-year-old man with a history of alcohol use disorder, COPD, and hypertension, was admitted after being found unresponsive in a T station with hypoxemia in the 80s on room air. He was started on high-flow oxygen, IV antibiotics, and steroids for suspected COPD exacerbation or pneumonia. His condition improved, and by the next morning, he was saturating well on room air. However, he refused further treatment, declined labs and exams, and insisted on leaving against medical advice before a Section 35 hold could be filed. He demonstrated capacity to make that decision and was discharged home with instructions to seek care if symptoms worsened.
problems: Acute alcoholic intoxication in alcoholism, continuous
